artworks.title: Clio, Euterpe and Thalia
artworks.description: Painted for the cabinet de l'Amour of the Hôtel Lambert in Paris and now in the Musée du Louvre, this canvas groups three of the nine Muses in a serene woodland. At the center sits Euterpe, Muse of music and lyric song, identified by the wind instrument she holds — the reed pipe descended from the ancient aulos that is her constant attribute — flanked by Clio with her book of history and Thalia with the mask of comedy. Le Sueur's restrained classicism makes Euterpe the harmonious pivot of the trio, embodying the music that the Greeks held the Muses to inspire in poets and singers.

artworks.title: Euterpe, the Muse of Music and Lyric Poetry
artworks.description: A Baroque single-figure portrayal by Simon Vouet, court painter to Louis XIII, isolating Euterpe from her eight sisters to celebrate her alone. The Muse of music and lyric poetry is shown absorbed in playing a wind instrument, the Renaissance and Baroque heir to the double flute (aulos) that classical tradition assigned her. Vouet's warm palette and turning, sculptural pose give the abstract personification a living presence, presenting Euterpe as the divine source of melody whom poets invoked for inspiration.

artworks.title: The Muse Euterpe
artworks.description: From Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Elder's series of the Nine Muses (1782), this Neoclassical study depicts Euterpe as Muse of music. Following the iconographic convention codified since antiquity, Tischbein equips her with a flute — the modern stand-in for the aulos, her traditional emblem — marking her out as the one star among the nine-Muse cluster who governs instrumental song. The painting reflects the eighteenth-century revival of the Muses as embodiments of the individual arts, with Euterpe presiding specifically over music and lyric melody.
